# Verify

Separate what is known from what was generated, before it leaves the building.

If `plumbward-profile.md` exists in the working folder, read it first. `## Work` says who the audience is — when it includes clients, courts, or regulators, apply the high-stakes procedure below by default. `## Guardrails` Always/Never lines are rules for what gets checked ("always cite sources" means every claim needs one). Treat each entry under `## Failure modes to prevent` as a standing rule — "confidently wrong on facts" written there means this skill is the answer to it. If no profile exists, proceed with the defaults below and do not mention the file.

The cost asymmetry here is extreme. A fabricated citation in a filing, a wrong figure in a client report, or an invented quote in a published piece costs vastly more than the minute it takes to check. Courts have sanctioned lawyers over exactly this.

## What always gets checked

- **Citations and sources** — case names, article titles, authors, publication dates, URLs, page numbers, statute and section numbers.
- **Numbers** — figures, percentages, currency, dates, counts, and anything derived from them.
- **Quotes** — anything in quotation marks attributed to a person or document.
- **Named entities** — people, companies, products, job titles, affiliations.
- **Claims about the present** — current prices, current holders of a role, whether something still exists, what is newest.

## The three-bucket pass

Before delivering, sort every checkable claim:

**Verified** — traced to a source read in this session, or computed here and re-checked.
**Unverified** — checkable in principle but not checked here: a search or file read could settle it.
**Uncertain** — no specific source identifiable even in principle, or the sources found conflict.

Then act on each bucket:

- Verified → state it plainly.
- Unverified → verify it now if a search or file read can settle it. If it cannot be settled, mark it in the output.
- Uncertain → either remove it or flag it explicitly. Never let it pass silently.
- Checked and found **false** → correct it or remove it, and say so. A disproven claim is not "uncertain."

The output should contain no unmarked claim from the second or third bucket.

## Citations

Never write a citation from memory. This is the single highest-risk operation in the skill.

Plausible-looking fabricated citations are the characteristic failure: a real journal, a real-sounding author, a real-format volume and page number, and no such article. The format being correct is not evidence the source exists.

Rules:
- Every citation must trace to a source actually retrieved in this session, or to a document the user provided.
- If a source cannot be retrieved, say so: "I can't verify this citation — you'll need to confirm it before filing." Do not offer an approximation.
- Never reconstruct a URL from a pattern. Use the URL as retrieved.
- When quoting, the quoted text must appear verbatim in the retrieved source. If it cannot be located, do not present it as a quote.

## Numbers

- Recompute every derived figure rather than carrying it forward from earlier in the conversation. Errors propagate silently.
- For anything with more than a couple of steps, compute it in code rather than mentally. Show the calculation.
- Check that totals sum, percentages resolve sensibly, and units and currencies are consistent.
- Confirm the time period of every figure. A correct number for the wrong year is still wrong.
- Sanity-check magnitude. If a result is off by a factor of a thousand, it is usually a unit error.

## Present-day facts

Anything that can change since training — prices, leaders, availability, versions, whether a law or policy is current — must be searched, not recalled. Confidence about these is not evidence.

## How to mark uncertainty

In the body of the work, inline and specific:

> Revenue grew 34% year over year. **[Unverified — from the draft you sent; I couldn't find the source figure. Confirm before this goes out.]**

Not a blanket disclaimer at the bottom. Blanket disclaimers get ignored and protect nobody. The mark goes on the specific claim, where a reader will hit it.

## When the stakes are high

For anything filed with a court or regulator, published under the user's name, or sent to a client — verify each citation independently rather than in bulk, and say plainly what was and was not confirmable.

If independent verification is not possible in this environment, say that clearly rather than implying a check happened.

## Rules

- Never present an unverified claim with the same confidence as a verified one.
- "It looks right" is not verification.
- If asked to verify and nothing can be checked in this environment, say so — do not perform a verification theater pass and report it as done.
- Report what was checked and what was not, briefly, so the user knows the boundary of the assurance.

# Darien Scheme — fact sheet SCAFFOLD

**STATUS: NOT PUBLISHABLE. NO CLAIM BELOW HAS BEEN VERIFIED.**

No source was retrieved while producing this document. Web access was unavailable
in the session that generated it. Every line below is recalled, not checked.
Citations are deliberately absent — see "Leads to check" at the end for the works
to verify against, which are themselves recalled and may be wrong.

Confidence tags:
- [FIRM] — widely repeated in the standard accounts; still needs a source before print.
- [SOFT] — I recall this but the specific figure/date may be wrong.
- [CONTESTED] — historians actively disagree. Do not print as settled fact.

---

## Core chronology

- [FIRM] The Company of Scotland Trading to Africa and the Indies was created by an
  Act of the Parliament of Scotland in 1695.
- [FIRM] The venture aimed to plant a colony on the Isthmus of Panama, in the Darien
  region, named New Caledonia.
- [FIRM] English capital was withdrawn from the company under political pressure —
  English Parliament and East India Company opposition — forcing the money to be
  raised inside Scotland. This is the fact that makes the "national exposure" angle
  work, and it is the one most worth nailing down precisely.
- [SOFT] First expedition sailed from Leith in July 1698; roughly five ships, roughly
  1,200 settlers; landed at Darien around November 1698.
- [SOFT] The first settlement was abandoned around July 1699 — disease, hunger,
  Spanish hostility, and an English colonial embargo on supplying the settlers.
- [SOFT] A second expedition arrived after the abandonment, was besieged by Spanish
  forces, and surrendered in the first half of 1700.
- [SOFT] Deaths across both expeditions are usually given as roughly 2,000 of about
  2,500 who sailed. The ratio is quoted more confidently than the underlying
  muster records support — check before printing a precise figure.

## The money

- [SOFT] Subscriptions are conventionally given as about £400,000 sterling.
  **Critical distinction to resolve:** subscribed (pledged) vs. actually paid up.
  I recall a paid-up figure materially lower than £400,000, but I do not trust my
  recollection of it. Printing the pledge figure as if it were money lost is a
  common error in popular accounts.
- [SOFT] The Equivalent paid to Scotland under the 1707 Union — a sum in the region
  of £398,000 — included compensation to Company of Scotland shareholders. The
  exact figure carries shillings and pence in the primary sources; get it exact
  or round it openly.

## The claim you specifically asked for

**"Share of Scotland's liquid capital" — [CONTESTED]. This is the single most
dangerous number in the piece.**

The traditional claim, repeated across popular histories and journalism, is that the
scheme absorbed somewhere between a quarter and a half of Scotland's liquid capital.
That range is doing enormous work on very thin evidence, and it has been challenged
by modern scholarship on at least three grounds:

1. There was no reliable measure of Scottish national wealth in the 1690s, so the
   denominator is itself an estimate.
2. Pledged capital and paid-up capital are frequently conflated, inflating the
   numerator.
3. The figure appears to have been repeated between secondary sources far more often
   than it has been independently recomputed.

If your piece leans on a single number, this is the one a specialist reader will
write in about. Recommended handling: attribute the range explicitly to whoever
you find actually asserting it, state the basis, and note that it is disputed —
rather than presenting it in your own voice as established fact.

## Leads to check (NOT citations — author/title recalled, unverified)

These are starting points for your own search, not sources I have read or confirmed.
Titles, authors, publishers and years below may be inaccurate.

- Douglas Watt — a book-length study of Darien's finances, published in the mid-2000s.
  I recall this as the main revisionist account that interrogates the capital figures
  directly. If only one thing gets checked, check this one: it likely contains the
  actual arithmetic behind the contested share.
- T. M. Devine — general history of the Scottish nation covering this period.
- John Prebble — narrative history of the Darien disaster, 1960s. Vivid and
  influential; older, and the place where several of the widely repeated figures
  probably entered general circulation.
- The National Records of Scotland and the Company of Scotland's own subscription
  ledgers, for the paid-up-vs-subscribed distinction at source.
- Recent peer-reviewed economic history of pre-Union Scotland, for the denominator.

## Before this runs

1. Confirm the paid-up capital figure from a primary or archival source.
2. Confirm the total subscription figure and label it as pledged, not lost.
3. Locate whoever actually asserts the liquid-capital share, and cite them by name
   rather than stating the range as fact.
4. Get exact dates for both expeditions' departures and the surrender.
5. Source the death toll or replace it with a sourced range.

## What I can't do

Zero sources retrieved. So: **no citations.** Not approximate ones, not "probably Devine 1999." Every author/title/year/page I could give you would be reconstructed from memory in the correct format, which is exactly what makes fabricated citations survive an editor's eye and then blow up in public.

## The number you asked for is the one to worry about

The "share of Scotland's liquid capital" figure — conventionally given as somewhere between a quarter and a half — is the most contested claim in this whole topic, not a settled fact you can drop in with a citation. It's weak on three counts:

- **The denominator doesn't exist.** There's no reliable measure of Scottish national wealth in the 1690s. The baseline is itself an estimate.
- **The numerator is usually wrong.** Popular accounts conflate *subscribed* (pledged) capital with *paid-up* capital. The conventional ~£400,000 sterling is a pledge figure; the money actually collected was materially lower. Presenting the pledge as "money Scotland lost" is the standard error.
- **It's been copied, not recomputed.** The range propagated between secondary sources far more often than anyone re-derived it.

There's a revisionist literature — I associate it with a mid-2000s book-length study by Douglas Watt specifically on Darien's finances — that goes after these numbers directly. I can't confirm the title, publisher or year, and you shouldn't print them on my say-so. But if you check one thing, check that: it likely contains the actual arithmetic.

A specialist reader will write in about this number. Safest handling: attribute the range to whoever you find actually asserting it, state its basis, and note it's disputed — rather than asserting it in your own voice.

## Recalled, unverified, for your own checking only

Firm-ish: Company of Scotland created by Act of the Scottish Parliament, 1695. Colony at Darien on the Isthmus of Panama, named New Caledonia. English capital withdrawn under Parliament/East India Company pressure, forcing domestic fundraising — this is the fact that makes the national-exposure angle work, so nail it down precisely.

Softer, verify every figure: first expedition sailed Leith July 1698, ~5 ships, ~1,200 settlers, landed ~November 1698; abandoned ~July 1699 under disease, hunger, Spanish hostility and an English colonial supply embargo; second expedition besieged and surrendered in the first half of 1700; deaths usually given as ~2,000 of ~2,500 — quoted more confidently than the muster records support. The 1707 Equivalent, around £398,000, included compensation to Company shareholders; the primary sources carry shillings and pence, so get it exact or round openly.

Other names worth searching, recalled and unverified: T. M. Devine's general history of the Scottish nation; John Prebble's 1960s narrative of the disaster (influential, and probably where several widely repeated figures entered circulation); the Company's own subscription ledgers at the National Records of Scotland for the paid-up-versus-subscribed split.

## If you want a real fact sheet tonight

Grant web access and re-run this — I'll verify each citation independently and tell you plainly which ones held up. That's maybe fifteen minutes of checking.

Otherwise: what's above is a research scaffold, not copy. Please don't let any of it run as-is under your name.
